2611.30328.abs: Autoregressive video diffusion models enable streaming synthesis chunk by chunk, yet invoking the large model for every chunk remains costly. While chunk-level speculative decoding can offload chunks to a lightweight draft model, existing approaches suffer from two limitations: (1) an off-the-shelf draft diverges from the target's trajectory, compounding errors in history; and (2) they either omit verification or rely on costly post-decode aesthetic scores rather than verifying consistency against the target. We address both with Draft Forcing, a framework coupling target-guided drafting with an on-policy trained verifier. Specifically, to align the draft for high acceptance, we opt for feature-level drafting, conditioning it on multi-layer target hidden states persisted from committed chunks, whose outputs are pushed to match target trajectories with multi-aspect losses. For verification, we propose an on-policy trained feature-space verifier predicting CDF-calibrated frame-wise relative RMSE against the target. It is trained on speculative rollouts as contexts anneal from random to inference-aligned mixtures, and gates proposals without VAE decoding. On the 14B Self-Forcing target, Draft Forcing achieves $1.63\times$ DiT and $1.57\times$ end-to-end speedups on VBench with minimal quality loss, and up to $1.93\times$ DiT ($1.82\times$ end-to-end) when combined with orthogonal KV compression. It generalizes to accelerate a streaming variant of MiniMax-H3, generating over $50\%$ draft frames with competitive quality.

2611.30889.abs: Can foundation models pretrained for generic numerical prediction serve as in-context robot learners? We investigate this question through tabular foundation models (TFMs), which are pretrained to infer input-output relationships from labeled examples in context. We introduce TabAct, which casts visual imitation as numerical prediction: frozen visual features and robot proprioception form the inputs, future action chunks form the targets, and each demonstration time step provides one labeled example that conditions a frozen TFM for closed-loop control. The predictor receives no robot-specific training or target-task fine-tuning. With one target-task demonstration available to each method, TabAct with TabICLv2 achieves the highest average success among all evaluated methods on both LIBERO and Meta-World, exceeding the strongest baseline by 20.9 and 5.8 percentage points, respectively. Additional demonstrations improve control without updating model weights: with five demonstrations, success reaches 94.2% on LIBERO-Object. These results demonstrate that generic numerical pretraining can provide an effective foundation for in-context robot learning.

2611.30405.abs: Large language model (LLM) coding agents operating on Web development platforms can interact with repositories, issue trackers, and continuous integration services to carry out long-horizon software engineering tasks. However, behavioral drift remains a major bottleneck in such multi-turn reasoning and action trajectories. To mitigate this, activation steering has emerged as a promising approach for regularizing agent behaviors by intervening on the LLM's transformer residual streams. Nonetheless, existing methods typically apply a static steering policy across all tasks, overlooking the fact that a single policy is rarely effective across heterogeneous tasks and varying execution turns. This limitation motivates dynamic online selection among candidate steering policies. Yet, doing so in long-horizon agentic settings is challenging: verifiable task-level feedback is only revealed upon task completion, leaving the contributions of individual steering turns unobserved. To address this challenge, we formulate online steering-policy selection as a multi-armed bandit problem with delayed task-level feedback and turn-level predictive hints derived from residual-stream activations. Within this formulation, we introduce Online Optimistic Activation Steering, a meta-framework that uses hints to guide within-task steering policy selection and leverages terminal task-level feedback to correct cumulative reward estimates. Theoretically, against the best fixed policy in hindsight, we prove regret bounds that tighten with increasing hint accuracy and establish a matching lower bound…

2611.29988.abs: Large language models (LLMs) answer many diet and health questions but can state unsupported claims and cite sources that do not support them. We present SHAKTI (Smart Health Advisor for Knowledge-based Tailored Interventions), a conversational assistant that answers only from retrieved scholarly papers and exact food-composition data, and evaluate it with retrieval, generation, grounding, efficiency and contextawareness metrics. We indexed 484,368,086 OpenAlex works, searched exactly on a GPU for evaluation (10,065 NFCorpus, BioASQ, SciFact and PubMedQA questions) and through a compressed 230-million-abstract index in deployment. On 1,000 stratified questions, we compared single-shot, multi-hop, corrective and deep-research retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with Claude Sonnet. SHAKTI adds conversational query rewriting, USDA FoodData Central lookups, source-link checks and online verification of quotes and numbers. It was tested in 36 scripted conversational turns, a 248-question memory-depth test and a 38-question load test. Claims were checked by a Claude Opus judge against exactly the text the system saw. MedCPT reranking of hybrid retrieval gave the best MRR (0.21) and MAP@100 (0.14). Across existing RAG methods, faithfulness was 0.95-0.96, claim hallucination 0.5-0.8% and context precision up to 0.98; the deep-research agent answered 73.2% of BioASQ questions correctly. In conversation, SHAKTI reached a context-awareness score of 97.1%, faithfulness 95.5%, 1.9% unsupported claims, no contradicted claims and 229/229 working source links; it resolved references to…

2611.30516.abs: Demonstrations show how a task can be completed, but differences in embodiment, appearance, and execution speed make it difficult to identify the guidance relevant to the robot's current progress. We introduce JEPA-ICL, a vision-language-action framework that couples predictive planning with demonstration learning. The policy learns to plan by predicting ordered future states in JEPA feature space up to subtask completion, capturing what remains to be accomplished. These plans guide action generation and locate relevant stages in demonstrations, whose JEPA-supervised content features provide progress-aligned context. Learning from this context, in turn, updates the shared policy that produces the plans and actions. This coupling connects anticipating the robot's own execution with reusing demonstrated experience. On the Imitator Game, JEPA-ICL achieves 80.0% seen-task success under C15 pretraining, outperforming Zero-WAM by 12.0 percentage points. Without contextual demonstrations, JEPA-ICL outperforms the VLA-JEPA variant without human-video pretraining, improving success rates from 96.1% to 97.6% on LIBERO and from 62.9% to 73.2% on LIBERO-Plus. With demonstration-based training and contextual guidance at inference, LIBERO-Plus success further increases from 73.2% to 75.2%.

2611.29619.abs: Most LLM agent frameworks build a crew that runs a task and exits. Physical environments (e.g., homes, labs, factory floors) need agents that stay up for months, survive their own bugs, and run on whatever hardware is already next to the sensors. We present Wactorz, an open-source runtime in which LLM-generated agents are long-lived, supervised actors: a planner turns a chat request into Python, compiles it into a new actor at runtime, and a supervisor restarts that actor alone, with its state intact, when it crashes. All coordination rides on MQTT, so agents can be spawned on, and live-migrated between, edge nodes such as a Raspberry Pi, and every internal event is a topic external systems can subscribe to. The recorded demo builds a camera-to-lamp automation from one chat request, adds a second agent that is auto-wired to the first by topic and carries a deliberate division-by-zero, watches that agent repair its own code without losing its count, then deploys a fresh Raspberry Pi node and live-migrates the agent onto it, in under four minutes of wall-clock time and \$0.13 of model usage. This extended version adds what the two-page demonstration paper could not: the Wiring view of the topic graph, Wactorz as a library for hand-written agents, how trained models are stored, sent to nodes and replaced, the security model, and the system's limitations.

2611.30130.abs: Rendering long text as images lets a vision-language model (VLM) read a document with fewer input tokens, and evaluations often count mainly these prefill tokens. We show that for reasoning models this accounting is incomplete. Across five models and two long-context benchmarks, reading the rendered document makes the model think longer: decode length grows by 1.5-3.5x on the four general-purpose VLMs tested, and under typical output pricing this decode tax makes image input more expensive than text for two of the five models on QuALITY. Unrecoverable information loss is not sufficient to explain the tax at moderate compression: Qwen's OCR of the same images recovers 98.7% of words, and feeding Kimi-K3 its own transcription as text restores text-mode reasoning length and accuracy. Whether compression pays off reduces to an exchange rate, (1-1/c)/(r-1), that must exceed the workload's price-weighted ratio of output to input tokens; this accounting decomposition shows why Kimi-K3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash can benefit and Qwen and GLM cannot. None of the training-free signals we test predicts the tax before generation. As a practical heuristic, an image-first policy that sends only inputs with a per-input compression ratio of at least 1.6 to images and falls back to text once image-mode reasoning costs as much as the input's prefill saving cuts the bill by 6-14% on Kimi-K3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at an accuracy cost of 0.3-1.2 points; on QuALITY, asking for a reasoning budget on both paths is a stronger lever.

ov.problema: Nei modelli VLM che ragionano, rendere il testo come immagine riduce i token di input, ma si trascura che il modello poi genera più token di output (decode), aumentando il costo. Questo è importante perché la compressione ottica potrebbe non convenire economicamente.
ov.idea: Gli autori analizzano il costo totale considerando sia i token di input che quelli di output. Introducono un tasso di cambio (1-1/c)/(r-1) che deve superare il rapporto prezzo-ponderato output/input del carico di lavoro. Propongono una politica 'image-first' che manda a immagini solo input con rapporto di compressione ≥1.6 e torna al testo quando il costo del ragionamento in modalità immagine supera il risparmio sui token di input.
ov.risultati: Su cinque modelli e due benchmark long-context, la lunghezza di decode cresce di 1.5-3.5x per i quattro VLM general-purpose. Su QuALITY, il costo extra rende l'input immagine più costoso del testo per due modelli su cinque. La politica image-first riduce il costo del 6-14% su Kimi-K3 e DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash con una perdita di accuratezza di 0.3-1.2 punti.
ov.limiti: Nessun segnale training-free testato predice il costo extra prima della generazione; la politica image-first è un'euristica e non sempre applicabile.

glossario.d: Vision-Language Model: modello che elabora sia testo che immagini.
Fase in cui il modello elabora i token di input prima di generare.
Fase di generazione dei token di output, uno alla volta.

2611.30617.abs: Geometry Problem Solving (GPS) serves as a rigorous test of the complex reasoning capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), particularly when solutions require auxiliary constructions absent from the input diagram. However, explicit diagramming methods suffer from unstable image generation quality and cascading errors, while existing implicit attention mechanisms primarily focus on visible elements, limiting their ability to support reasoning that requires additional geometric constructions. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{AuxCA} (Auxiliary-Clues-Aware GRPO), a reinforcement learning framework that helps models learn transferable auxiliary-construction strategies that can be applied beyond the training domain without explicit diagram generation at inference time. Specifically, we introduce Auxiliary Clues Dependency (\textbf{ACD}) to quantify the influence of auxiliary visual clues on token generation and integrate it into GRPO through fine-grained advantage weighting. Furthermore, we incorporate an auxiliary incentive reward to encourage the effective use of auxiliary geometric clues in correct solutions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AuxCA-8B outperforms the explicit-plotting baseline Bagel-Canvas and achieves competitive performance with leading proprietary models on auxiliary-dependent plane geometry problems. Improvements on analytic geometry, solid geometry, and external benchmarks further suggest that the learned strategies can transfer beyond the training domain. Code is available at https://github.com/fukua23/AuxCA

2611.31099.abs: Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $π_{0.5}$ re-encode the camera images and the instruction with a 2B-parameter backbone at every control step, and the feed-forward layers of this prefix account for most of its compute. A natural way to save this compute is to send most tokens through a low-rank MLP and compute exactly only the tokens whose approximation error is large. We find that this intuition is wrong. Even a verifier that knows every token's exact error picks the wrong tokens, producing 1.3--1.7$\times$ larger action deviation than a simple test of whether a token's input is novel, that is, whether it falls outside the subspace seen during calibration. Large errors concentrate in tokens the policy relies on little, such as the third-person camera, while the novelty test favors the wrist camera, a view the action depends on heavily. We call this the error--reliance gap. Building on it, we propose NoveltyGate, a training-free method that routes each prefix token, once per layer and before any multiplication, to either a low-rank or the original MLP. Deciding once per layer instead of once per matrix product avoids moving wide intermediate tensors and keeps every shape static, so the whole prefix runs as a single CUDA graph. On LIBERO, NoveltyGate accelerates the $π_{0.5}$ prefix by up to 1.61$\times$, stays 2.7--2.9$\times$ closer to the original policy than channel pruning and low-rank compression at equal compute, and preserves closed-loop task success.

ov.problema: I modelli visione-linguaggio-azione (VLA) con flow-matching come π0.5 ricodificano immagini e istruzioni con un backbone da 2 miliardi di parametri a ogni passo di controllo, e i layer feed-forward del prefisso consumano la maggior parte del calcolo. Un modo naturale per risparmiare è mandare la maggior parte dei token attraverso un MLP a basso rango e calcolare esattamente solo quelli con errore di approssimazione grande.
ov.idea: Gli autori trovano che questa intuizione è sbagliata: anche un verificatore che conosce l'errore esatto di ogni token sceglie i token sbagliati, producendo una deviazione dell'azione 1,3-1,7 volte maggiore rispetto a un semplice test di novità dell'input (se cade fuori dal sottospazio visto in calibrazione). I grandi errori si concentrano in token che la politica usa poco, come la telecamera in terza persona, mentre il test di novità favorisce la telecamera del polso, una vista da cui l'azione dipende molto. Questo è il divario errore-affidabilità. NoveltyGate è un metodo training-free che…
ov.risultati: Su LIBERO, NoveltyGate accelera il prefisso di π0.5 fino a 1,61 volte, resta 2,7-2,9 volte più vicino alla politica originale rispetto a channel pruning e compressione a basso rango a pari calcolo, e preserva il compito in closed-loop.
ov.limiti: Il testo si interrompe prima di elencare eventuali limiti.

glossario.d: modello che collega visione, linguaggio e azione per controllare robot
tecnica generativa che apprende un campo di flusso per trasformare distribuzioni
rete feed-forward con matrici di peso di rango ridotto per risparmiare calcolo

2611.30742.abs: Large language model (LLM) agents are often ranked by an LLM judge whose error rates are measured once and reused for every agent. The corrected success rates can then be biased when the judge's errors depend on the trajectory and agents differ in the trajectories they produce for successes or failures. We derive the exact asymptotic bias and give a chain of checks from identification to simultaneous ranks. On a four-agent semi-synthetic benchmark, a scalar correction with oracle calibration has maximum bias 0.245 and mean pointwise coverage 0.016, and never recovers the full ranking (0/250 replications). Augmented inverse-probability weighting (AIPW) with a uniform or a design-aware random audit keeps the maximum bias below 0.003, with mean pointwise coverage of 0.939 and 0.950. In a 48-cell stress test, effective target support rises only from 0.209 to 0.805 as calibration grows from 600 to 4,800 labels, while audited AIPW keeps a mean absolute error of 0.018-0.020. Without calibration support, or with judge dependence within an externally justified bound, we report valid bounds or sensitivity sets and carry them into rank sets. An e-process confidence sequence stays valid, for a stable target, under predictable adaptive auditing and arbitrary stopping.

ov.problema: Gli agenti LLM sono valutati da un giudice LLM, ma gli errori del giudice possono dipendere dalla traiettoria (sequenza di azioni) e gli agenti producono traiettorie diverse. Questo introduce distorsioni nelle classifiche.
ov.idea: Gli autori derivano la distorsione asintotica esatta e propongono una catena di controlli. Usano un aggiustamento con inverse-probability weighting aumentato (AIPW) e audit casuali (uniformi o design-aware) per correggere gli errori del giudice.
ov.risultati: Su un benchmark semi-sintetico a quattro agenti, la correzione scalare con calibrazione oracle ha bias massimo 0.245 e copertura media 0.016, e non recupera mai la classifica completa (0/250). AIPW con audit mantiene bias massimo sotto 0.003 e copertura 0.939-0.950. In stress test, AIPW mantiene errore assoluto medio 0.018-0.020.
ov.limiti: Senza supporto di calibrazione o con dipendenza dal giudice entro un limite esterno, si ottengono solo bound validi o set di sensibilità, non stime puntuali.

glossario.d: Metodo statistico che combina un modello e pesi per correggere distorsioni.
Percentuale di intervalli di confidenza che contengono il vero valore.
Sequenza di confidenza valida per test sequenziali con stop arbitrario.

2611.30613.abs: Open video generators such as MiniMax-H3 produce short clips of only several to a dozen seconds per run. To synthesize longer sequences, existing methods either rely on agentic systems following preset scripts, or roll out autoregressively from the previous clip's last frame, losing off-screen states and accumulating hallucinations across turns. Consequently, users still cannot take an explicit goal, choose how to accomplish it, and see that choice persist across subsequent clips. We study goal-grounded interactive video generation, where one goal admits multiple valid approaches, the user's chosen approach must be executed on screen, and its consequences must persist across clips. To this end, we propose CineAct, a state-first agentic framework in which language-model agents handle reasoning while frozen image and video generators serve purely as renderers. Before interaction, the Architect initializes the world as a spatial layout with cameras, an asset library, and a scene graph; at each turn, the system deduces the planned state change, generates a target end frame with an image generator and rigorously verifies it, and synthesizes intermediate motion with an FL2V model. We further introduce a multi-space benchmark covering two suites: long-horizon step execution and open-intent branching admissibility. Experiments show that explicit world-state modeling boosts multi-step rollout consistency over the pixel-only baseline (+11.4 automated, +23.1 human points) and raises paired branching success toward a shared goal by +30.8 points.

2611.30205.abs: Looped language models reuse one block of weights T times per token, trading parameters for test-time depth, but autoregressive decoding then pays T sequential passes per token. Self-speculative decoders recover 2-10x for a single request, yet their gains fade as requests share a GPU, and current practice is to speculate less as load grows. We show that what fails under load is the layout of speculative work, not speculation. In concurrent decoding the unit of cost is the row, one request advancing on one loop, which reads that loop's key-value (KV) cache once; additional positions inside a row are nearly free. Pipelined schedules such as the wavefront place every speculative position on a different loop, hence in a row of its own, so each token is still read T times. We present PackLoop, built on one principle: speculate only inside rows that are read anyway. Deep loops accumulate positions and advance them as a block in one row, context-copy proposals join the row that the first loop already reads, and a closed-form admission rule, the economic order quantity of inventory theory, sets how long to accumulate from a cost model calibrated once per engine. PackLoop is exact: in FP32 its output is token-for-token identical to autoregressive decoding, also under sampling and early exit. Across 164 load points spanning three GPUs, four Ouro models, six benchmarks, and contexts up to 32K tokens, one PackLoop configuration is faster than the best existing schedule, chosen per point, at 161 points (median 1.25x, up to 1.76x) and never significantly slower. Its lead grows with…

ov.problema: I modelli 'looped' riusano lo stesso blocco di pesi T volte per ogni token, ma la decodifica autoregressiva paga T passaggi sequenziali per token. I decoder self-speculative (che generano più token e li verificano) accelerano 2-10x su singola richiesta, ma il guadagno svanisce quando più richieste condividono la GPU.
ov.idea: Gli autori mostrano che sotto carico il problema è la disposizione del lavoro speculativo, non la speculazione in sé: l'unità di costo è la 'riga' (una richiesta che avanza su un loop, leggendo una volta la sua KV cache), e posizioni aggiuntive nella stessa riga costano quasi nulla. PackLoop specula solo dentro righe già lette: accumula posizioni nei loop profondi e le avanza come blocco in una riga, e una regola di ammissione chiusa (dalla teoria delle scorte) decide quanto accumulare.
ov.risultati: PackLoop è esatto: in FP32 l'output è identico token per token alla decodifica autoregressiva, anche con sampling ed early exit. Su 164 punti di carico (tre GPU, quattro modelli Ouro, sei benchmark, contesti fino a 32K token) una singola configurazione è più veloce della migliore schedulazione esistente scelta per punto.
ov.limiti: Il testo è troncato e non riporta i numeri di speedup effettivi.

glossario.d: Memoria dei key-value già calcolati per i token precedenti, riusata per non ricalcolarli.
Il modello propone più token e poi li verifica, accelerando la generazione.
Tecnica che interrompe prima il calcolo quando la risposta è già affidabile.

2611.30298.abs: Learning robust representations from electrocardiograms (ECGs) is challenging because repeated cardiac cycles coexist with subtle and sparse diagnostic cues in local morphology and rhythm-level context. Existing ECG foundation models commonly rely on Transformerbased patch encoders with uniformly shared dense refinement pathways, limiting adaptive processing across heterogeneous ECG tokens. We propose HEART (Hierarchical Expert Adaptive Refinement Transformer), an ECG foundation model that introduces stage-specific conditional expert refinement during self-supervised pre-training. HEART places a local-level MoE over patch-level representations before temporal contextualization and a global-level MoE over context-integrated token representations after self-attention. Token-level Top-1 routing allows different patches or contextual tokens within the same ECG to follow different expert pathways. On public ECG benchmarks, HEART achieves strong performance under both linear probing and fine-tuning, with particularly large frozen-encoder gains on PTB-XL Form and Rhythm (+6.76 AUROC points each over the strongest protocol-reproduced baseline). Routing analyses provide qualitative evidence of complementary local and global expert specialization. We release our code and pretrained models at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/HEART-5E9F.

2611.29877.abs: Video corpus moment retrieval (VCMR) requires finding the video and time interval that match a text query in a corpus of videos. We present RELAY, a training-free framework for VCMR that shares memory across queries. RELAY processes a batch of queries in three stages: search with a query bank, ranking with video notes, and localization with video prompt caching. In the search stage, an embedding model scores each video by its best-matching frame. The query bank penalizes videos that score highly for many other queries in the batch. In the ranking stage, a vision-language model (VLM) writes notes on each candidate video's scenes, people, objects, and actions once. Then, a large language model (LLM) reranks the candidates from these notes. In the localization stage, a VLM predicts the time interval of the moment in the top-ranked video. When multiple queries select the same video, prompt caching lets the VLM reuse its frames. On the three VERIFIED benchmarks, RELAY outperforms the trained baselines in video retrieval R@1 without training. Without any labeled moment, its predicted intervals are shorter than the annotated ones. In VCMR, it achieves similar performance to VideoSearch-R1 on one benchmark and trails it at IoU 0.5 on the other two. Human annotators also mark shorter moments than the original annotations of the benchmarks. A single margin, calibrated on a few labeled queries, widens the predicted interval to the annotation convention of the benchmarks. With it, RELAY outperforms the trained baselines in VCMR at IoU 0.5.

2611.30490.abs: Egocentric human manipulation data offer a scalable resource for training dexterous robot policies. However, how effectively robots can learn and benefit from these data remains unclear due to the embodiment gap between humans and robots. We present EgoStudy, a systematic, controlled study of egocentric data for robot learning. Holding the robot dataset fixed, we vary the scale and diversity of egocentric data, data processing strategies, and co-training configurations. We investigate three questions: (1) Which data processing and pretraining choices most effectively exploit egocentric data? (2) Which components of robot action prediction benefit most from scaling these data? (3) How do scaling effects differ between vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs)? Our experiments yield three main findings. First, data diversity, alignment between trajectories, and detailed language annotations are key factors in effective transfer. Second, scaling egocentric data yields larger gains in predicting end-effector translation than in predicting fine-grained finger movements. Third, WAMs perform better when egocentric data are limited, whereas VLAs exhibit greater gains as the amount of egocentric data increases. Together, these findings provide practical guidance on processing and using egocentric data to train VLAs and WAMs, while clarifying the benefits and limitations of scaling these data.

2611.29473.abs: Touchard and the author asked whether every valued hyperfield, in Krasner's sense with the norm axiom, is of the form H_ρ(K): a valued field K read up to relative error ρ. The question turns on the norm axiom. If a valued hyperfield is a quotient K^times/Tcup{0} of a field, the norm axiom forces T=1+m_ρ for a valuation on K. This completes the proof of a published proposition, and it makes the question equivalent to asking whether every Krasner valued hyperfield is such a quotient. For value group Z we prove directly that it is. Without the norm axiom the answer is negative. Layering a hyperfield over a non-trivial ordered abelian group gives a factor hyperfield exactly when the hyperfield itself is one, so Massouros's hyperfields yield hyperfields with a non-trivial valuation, satisfying all the other axioms, that are not factor hyperfields. The general question remains open.

2611.30017.abs: We present OWE-Bench (OpenWorldEngineer-Bench), a benchmark of 26 long-horizon engineering tasks written by domain experts in software engineering, physical engineering, machine learning, and scientific computing. Tasks range from optimizing kernels and designing an aircraft, to identifying the faults responsible for an earthquake. Each task requires significant domain knowledge and engineering work, with models averaging hundreds of millions of tokens per task. Solutions are scored on practical measures such as speed, cost and accuracy, both on provided cases the agent could test against and on hidden cases that an engineer would expect from the task description. The best-performing frontier model so far, Claude Fable 5.2, scores 54.6% and averages 211 million tokens per task. We highlight two findings. First, when models are given more time, they use more test-time compute and achieve higher scores. Models also scale differently with test-time compute: GPT-6 Astra achieves higher scores at shorter time limits and at equal token use, while Claude Fable 5.2 uses more tokens at longer limits to achieve the highest overall score. Second, each model scores lower on hidden cases than on the provided cases, by an average of 18 points, which we call the deployment gap. Models also fail to predict the deployment gap, overestimating their performance on hidden test cases by an average of 21 points. We hope that OWE-Bench grounds progress toward agents whose engineering solutions perform as well in deployment as they do in testing.

ov.problema: Mancano benchmark per valutare agenti su compiti ingegneristici a lungo termine, che richiedono centinaia di milioni di token e competenze specialistiche. Questo è importante per misurare progressi reali verso agenti utili in ingegneria.
ov.idea: OWE-Bench contiene 26 compiti scritti da esperti in software, ingegneria fisica, ML e calcolo scientifico. I modelli sono valutati su casi forniti e casi nascosti, con metriche pratiche come velocità, costo e accuratezza. Si analizza come i modelli scalano con il tempo di test e il divario tra casi forniti e nascosti.
ov.risultati: Il miglior modello, Claude Fable 5.2, ottiene il 54.6% e consuma in media 211 milioni di token per compito. I modelli usano più token con più tempo e migliorano i punteggi, ma ogni modello segna in media 18 punti in meno sui casi nascosti (deployment gap) e sovrastima la propria performance di 21 punti.
ov.limiti: Il benchmark è limitato a 26 compiti e i modelli non riescono a prevedere il proprio divario di deployment.

glossario.d: Compiti che richiedono molte interazioni e molto tempo per essere completati.
Risorse di calcolo usate durante l'esecuzione del modello, come token generati.
Differenza di prestazioni tra casi di test forniti e casi nascosti.

2611.30603.abs: The Divan hay vimagrut'yan (1960-2017), the printed corpus of Armenian inscriptions, comprises nearly 7,600 records; a growing number of the inscriptions they describe, damaged or destroyed in recent decades, survive only in its pages. Armenian epigraphy nevertheless lacks a digital resource of the kind available for Greek, Latin or Georgian. This paper presents the Corpus Inscriptionum Armenicarum Electronicum, which turns the ten volumes of the Divan into an open digital corpus. Layout detection, OCR and a vision-language model produce a first structured reading of each record, which specialists then check on a proofreading platform. First corrections show that letters are read reliably and that residual errors concentrate in the editorial signs. The corpus is designed as a lasting platform for documenting Armenian inscriptions and as a source of silver data in Classical and Middle Armenian for language models and computational linguistics.

2611.31065.abs: Hard token budgets often interrupt LLM reasoning before an answer is produced. Forcing reasoning to terminate recovers correct solutions but also increases confident errors, creating a joint challenge of solving within budget and deciding when to abstain. Existing remedies are costly or lack guarantees: supervised fine-tuning offers no error control, penalizing wrong answers during reinforcement learning (RL) can suppress exploration, and multi-sample conformal methods multiply inference cost. We propose Tail-CRC, a single-rollout framework that separates candidate generation from submission control. We first adapt the solver to budget forcing with pure binary correctness rewards; after freezing it, we apply conformal risk control to upper-tail token surprise in the answer span. Each rollout yields both an answer and an uncertainty score from token log probabilities, enabling finite-sample control of expected wrong submissions under exchangeability and recalibration across risk targets or domains without retraining. We show that wrong-answer penalties create failure-only comparisons in group-relative RL, derive an exploration-starvation boundary, and identify length-induced ranking reversals and single-token spike sensitivity in answer scores. Across Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3-8B, 50 RL updates on 400 problems improve correct-submission rates by 15.0--29.6 points on DAPO and 4.3--12.8 points on out-of-domain Omni-MATH over inference-only budget forcing, while reducing generation cost by 3.5--12.6\%. On 8B Omni-MATH, target-domain calibration cuts wrong submissions from 30.3\% to…

ov.problema: I modelli linguistici di grandi dimensioni (LLM) spesso interrompono il ragionamento prima di produrre una risposta quando hanno un budget limitato di token. Forzare la terminazione recupera soluzioni corrette ma aumenta gli errori sicuri, creando la sfida di risolvere entro il budget e decidere quando astenersi.
ov.idea: Tail-CRC separa la generazione delle risposte dal controllo di sottomissione. Prima adatta il risolutore a forzare il budget con ricompense binarie di correttezza; poi, congelato il risolutore, applica il controllo del rischio conformale (metodo statistico per garantire un limite di errore) sull'incertezza dei token nella risposta. Ogni rollout produce una risposta e un punteggio di incertezza dalle probabilità dei token, permettendo un controllo a campione finito degli errori attesi.
ov.risultati: Su Qwen3.5-4B e Qwen3-8B, 50 aggiornamenti RL su 400 problemi migliorano i tassi di sottomissione corretta di 15.0-29.6 punti su DAPO e 4.3-12.8 punti su Omni-MATH fuori dominio rispetto al forzare il budget solo in inferenza, riducendo la generazione di...
ov.limiti: Il metodo richiede l'assunzione di scambiabilità (exchangeability) e potrebbe non funzionare bene se i dati non sono scambiabili.

glossario.d: Metodo statistico per garantire un limite di errore su nuove previsioni.
Una singola esecuzione del modello per generare una risposta.
Proprietà dei dati per cui l'ordine non conta per la distribuzione.

2611.30624.abs: LLM agents act through tool calls: the model writes the arguments of a call as JSON, a guard decides whether the call may run, and an executor runs it. The same bytes are parsed several times, by the provider, gateways, SDKs, frameworks, the guard, and the executor. JSON leaves some choices to each parser, such as which copy of a repeated key counts. When the guard and the executor choose differently, the guard approves one call, the executor runs another, and the audit log records the approved one. We introduce this attack, tool-call smuggling, and study it across the stack. We describe six ways in which the same bytes yield different calls and build a differential testing harness that gives identical bytes to 17 pinned parser and validator configurations; most pairs disagree on some inputs, and even two official MCP SDKs accept different inputs. On tasks from $τ$-bench and AgentDojo, an attacker who can rewrite the bytes in transit cancels another customer's reservation and creates a file that the guard blocks by name, while the audit log names only the approved call. Content the model reads splits guard and executor only inside a string: ten models we test write no repeated or disguised key into the call itself where we see it, but copy one verbatim into JSON text in an argument, which a Python guard and a Go executor read differently. A malicious server copying a legitimate tool's public schema and adding one field, which a note explains, gets the model to fill it, unseen by the guard, with user data. Parsing each call once, JSON text included, keeping only the fields…

ov.problema: Gli agenti LLM agiscono tramite chiamate a strumenti: il modello scrive gli argomenti come JSON, un guard decide se la chiamata può essere eseguita e un executor la esegue. Gli stessi byte vengono analizzati più volte da parser diversi, e JSON lascia alcune scelte a ciascun parser, come quale copia di una chiave ripetuta conta. Quando guard e executor scelgono diversamente, il guard approva una chiamata, l'executor ne esegue un'altra e il log di audit registra quella approvata.
ov.idea: Gli autori introducono questo attacco, chiamato tool-call smuggling, e lo studiano su tutto lo stack. Descrivono sei modi in cui gli stessi byte producono chiamate diverse e costruiscono un harness di test differenziale che fornisce byte identici a 17 configurazioni di parser e validatori.
ov.risultati: La maggior parte delle coppie di parser è in disaccordo su alcuni input, e persino due SDK MCP ufficiali accettano input diversi. Su task di τ-bench e AgentDojo, un attaccante che può riscrivere i byte in transito cancella la prenotazione di un altro cliente e crea un file che il guard blocca per nome, mentre il log di audit nomina solo la chiamata approvata. Dieci modelli testati non scrivono chiavi ripetute o camuffate nella chiamata stessa, ma ne copiano una verbatim nel testo JSON di un argomento, che un guard Python e un executor Go leggono diversamente.

glossario.d: Chiamata a funzione esterna fatta da un agente LLM, con argomenti in JSON.
Programma che interpreta una stringa di testo secondo una sintassi.
Componente che decide se una chiamata a strumento può essere eseguita.

2611.30607.abs: Generating realistic 3D human object interactions (HOI) is essential for applications, such as augmented or virtual reality (AR/VR) or character animation of interactive entertainment. A particular challenge lies in the faithful generation of hand grasps in human object interaction scenes, where even minor geometric inconsistencies, such as insufficient contact or interpenetration, can significantly compromise realism. While diffusion-based generative models have shown promising results in HOI synthesis, ensuring physically plausible hand-object interactions remains challenging. We present Tri-DNO, a diffusion noise optimization strategy to sample from a pretrained multimodal HOI diffusion model, improving hand-object contact. Rather than modifying or retraining the generative model, our approach iteratively optimizes the initial noise of the diffusion generator, thereby generating firm hand object contact, while mitigating penetration and keeping the hand position realistic. Experiments on the GRAB dataset demonstrate improvements over the baseline in grasp quality without additional model training or increased computational cost compared to existing methods. We further demonstrate the applicability of our approach to practical media production scenarios.

2611.30195.abs: World action models guide robots by predicting the effects of actions or generating commands from observations. A model may compare hundreds of candidate futures before acting, repeatedly reading weights that must fit in device memory. Post-training quantization reduces the number of bits used to store pretrained weights, but a smaller model is not necessarily a deployable one: temporary tensors can exceed graphics processing unit (GPU) memory limits, while even small prediction errors can change the selected action. This creates two coupled challenges: identifying bit assignments that preserve task performance and determining which of them meet real execution constraints, without exhausting costly task trials. We present PTQ4WAM, a framework for choosing layer-wise bit assignments and execution routes under memory, latency and task-evaluation budgets. Calibration measurements guide candidate proposals, optionally with a language model agent. We profile full-model routes on the GPU before spending task trials on feasible assignments. Fusing group rescaling and reading visual history in place can make an otherwise infeasible assignment deployable. Across 15 workloads from four model families, the median task score is 99.2% of the corresponding 32-bit floating-point (FP32) score. On fixed GPU replays, the median speedup over FP32 is 2.36 times and the median reduction in peak allocated memory is 71.5%. The code will be released soon.

ov.problema: Nei world action models per robot, la quantizzazione post-training riduce i bit dei pesi, ma un modello più piccolo non è necessariamente deployabile: tensori temporanei possono superare la memoria GPU e piccoli errori di predizione possono cambiare l'azione scelta.
ov.idea: PTQ4WAM è un framework che sceglie assegnazioni di bit per layer e percorsi di esecuzione sotto vincoli di memoria, latenza e budget di valutazione. Misurazioni di calibrazione guidano le proposte, opzionalmente con un agente LLM, e i percorsi full-model vengono profilati sulla GPU prima di spendere prove sul task.
ov.risultati: Su 15 workload di quattro famiglie di modelli, il punteggio mediano sul task è il 99.2% di quello FP32. Su replay GPU fissi, lo speedup mediano rispetto a FP32 è 2.36x e la riduzione mediana della memoria di picco allocata è del 71.5%.
ov.limiti: Il codice sarà rilasciato presto; i risultati sono su workload specifici e non è chiaro quanto generalizzino ad altri modelli o hardware.

glossario.d: Riduzione della precisione dei pesi di un modello già addestrato.
Formato a virgola mobile a 32 bit, precisione standard.
Tempo di risposta o esecuzione di un'operazione.

2611.30151.abs: Continual learning in language models is commonly studied in the incremental learning (IL) setting, where a model learns a sequence of tasks and is evaluated through its final classifier or language-model (LM) head. This interface, however, does not indicate where forgetting occurs: a drop in accuracy may reflect representation degradation in the backbone, readout mismatch in the head, or both. We therefore argue that backward transfer (BWT) and forward transfer (FWT) should be interpreted as interface-dependent quantities rather than as single modellevel properties. We study three evaluation interfaces: the trained head, which is updated sequentially with the backbone; a probe newly trained on frozen backbone features; and a classifier-free backbone diagnostic. They measure deployed performance, recoverability under a new readout, and representation separability, respectively. Across class-incremental experiments with encoder and decoder language backbones, plus task-incremental sanity checks, conclusions about forgetting and plasticity change with the interface: the trained head often indicates severe forgetting, the probe near-complete recoverability, and the backbone diagnostic intermediate representation drift with a consistent negative relation between stability and plasticity. This relation holds for clustering-free diagnostics such as nearest-class-mean accuracy and across five clustering algorithms and three metrics. Finally, Just LM-Head Tuning (JLT), a head-only intervention on a fixed incrementally trained backbone, recovers 96-99% of the gap to joint training…

ov.problema: L'apprendimento continuo nei modelli linguistici è studiato tipicamente nell'apprendimento incrementale, valutato tramite il classificatore finale o l'head del modello. Questa interfaccia non indica dove avviene la dimenticanza: un calo di accuratezza può riflettere degradazione della rappresentazione nel backbone, disallineamento nell'head, o entrambi.
ov.idea: Gli autori sostengono che il trasferimento all'indietro (BWT) e in avanti (FWT) dovrebbero essere interpretati come quantità dipendenti dall'interfaccia. Studiano tre interfacce: l'head addestrato (aggiornato sequenzialmente con il backbone), una probe addestrata su feature congelate del backbone, e una diagnostica del backbone senza classificatore. Misurano rispettivamente performance deployata, recuperabilità con un nuovo readout, e separabilità della rappresentazione.
ov.risultati: In esperimenti class-incremental con backbone encoder e decoder, le conclusioni su dimenticanza e plasticità cambiano con l'interfaccia: l'head addestrato spesso indica grave dimenticanza, la probe quasi completa recuperabilità, e la diagnostica del backbone una deriva intermedia della rappresentazione con una relazione negativa costante tra stabilità e plasticità. Questa relazione vale per diagnostiche senza clustering come l'accuratezza nearest-class-mean e attraverso cinque algoritmi di clustering e tre metriche.
ov.limiti: Lo studio si concentra su specifici backbone e set di dati; i risultati potrebbero non generalizzare ad altri.

glossario.d: Effetto dell'apprendimento di nuovi compiti sulle performance sui compiti precedenti.
Effetto dell'apprendimento precedente sulle performance su nuovi compiti.
Classificatore semplice addestrato su feature congelate per valutare la rappresentazione.

2611.29829.abs: Agentic pipelines that combine graph detectors, deterministic rules, retrieval-augmented generation and an LLM judge are being proposed to monitor illicit cryptocurrency flows and to write regulation-citing justifications for analysts. They are evaluated on end-to-end accuracy or on the quality of those justifications, and neither shows which component made a decision. We audit such a pipeline on the Elliptic++ Bitcoin dataset with decision-source attribution, a trace-level protocol with three layers: per-case actual causation, interventional Shapley credit, and mediation of upstream risk scores. A deterministic wallet-score override carries about 94% of the credit for flags, and a verification gate cancels most of the judge's own flags, which fall on licit transactions. Testing the judge alone over 76 evidence bundles, four backbones and two prompts, we find that it follows an injected risk score on the anonymous transaction features it is given, although stronger models decide correctly when the facts are explicit; that a context too short for the system prompt leaves it with no verdict at all; and that it cites regulatory clauses that do not apply, which a substring-based citation check accepts. Hiding the score does not fix the judge, because evidence gathered with the score visible still encodes it. For illicit-activity monitoring, an LLM's justification should therefore not be read as evidence of which component flagged a transaction.

2611.30477.abs: Flow-based vision-language-action models can benefit from robot experience collected during deployment, but repeatedly acquiring new physical interactions for policy improvement is costly. Offline reinforcement learning provides a natural way to reuse collected experience, while flow-based policies offer an additional opportunity because fresh generation trajectories can be cheaply resampled from the current policy at replay observations. This motivates separating offline value learning from on-policy optimization of the generative process. We propose OVOGO, an offline reinforcement learning framework that realizes this separation for flow-based VLAs. A central challenge in this formulation is to learn a critic that remains grounded in logged robot experience while providing useful value signals for newly generated actions. OVOGO introduces a Return-Anchored Ranking Critic that combines in-sample distributional value learning with guarded local ranking, improving discrimination among generated actions without assigning them artificial return targets. The frozen critic then provides group-relative value signals for selected-transition optimization of fresh action candidates sampled from the current flow policy. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, DexJoCo, and LIBERO, as well as a real-robot dexterous manipulation task, show that OVOGO improves the initial VLA across all four settings and achieves higher success rates than the evaluated offline adaptation and value-guided baselines. These results suggest that offline robot experience can be repeatedly reused for value learning…

2611.29006.abs: The decay exponent α in KV-cache eviction is an intrinsic property of the model: calibrated once on a single corpus, it transfers directly across domains. Attention-based accumulation (H2O) and recency-based sliding windows (StreamingLLM) are two dominant eviction frameworks, often treated as unrelated, but we show that they are the two endpoints of a single power-law family: by scoring each token as s_i = A_i cdot (t-i)^{-α}, where A_i is cumulative attention and α controls the age penalty, H2O and StreamingLLM correspond to α=0 and αtoinfty, respectively (with StreamingLLM additionally hard-coding an attention-sink patch). The no-hair mechanism of xiang2026nohair bounds the admissible range of α, and the measured exponents agree: calibrating once on WikiText yields [0.556, 0.822] for a representative model (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct). The per-model ranges are consistent across five models (410M--1.5B) and independently match the optimal regions from perplexity sweeps. NoHairCache achieves the lowest perplexity across three datasets (WikiText, PG19, and arXiv) without per-dataset tuning, outperforming both H2O and StreamingLLM (p < 0.05 on all three datasets, with 0.06--0.10 PPL gains over StreamingLLM at budget 512). On downstream four-way multiple-choice QA, it matches or outperforms StreamingLLM across all nine (task, budget) cells, retaining 98.2% of full-cache accuracy on NarrativeQA at 25% retention versus 91.1% for StreamingLLM; per-cell McNemar tests are not significant, so QA is corroborating only. We release our calibration script and drop-in scorer upon publication.

ov.problema: Nella generazione di testo con LLM, la KV cache (memoria dei token passati) cresce e va sfoltita; i metodi esistenti come H2O (basato sull'attenzione accumulata) e StreamingLLM (basato sulla recenza) sembrano diversi e richiedono tuning per dataset.
ov.idea: Gli autori mostrano che H2O e StreamingLLM sono due estremi di un'unica famiglia power-law: ogni token è scored come s_i = A_i * (t-i)^{-α}, dove A_i è l'attenzione cumulata e α penalizza l'età. H2O corrisponde ad α=0, StreamingLLM ad α→∞. L'esponente α è una proprietà intrinseca del modello: calibrandolo una volta su WikiText si ottiene un intervallo valido per tutti i domini.
ov.risultati: Calibrando una volta su WikiText si ottiene α in [0.556, 0.822] per Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, coerente su cinque modelli (410M–1.5B) e con gli sweep di perplessità. NoHairCache ha la perplessità più bassa su WikiText, PG19 e arXiv senza tuning per dataset, con guadagni di 0.06–0.10 PPL su StreamingLLM a budget 512 (p<0.05). Su QA a 4 scelte mantiene il 98.2% dell'accuratezza full-cache su NarrativeQA al 25% di retention (StreamingLLM 91.1%).
ov.limiti: I test McNemar per cella non sono significativi; i modelli testati sono piccoli (410M–1.5B).

glossario.d: Memoria dei token passati usata dagli LLM per generare il prossimo token senza ricalcolare tutto.
Relazione matematica in cui una quantità decresce come una potenza negativa di un'altra.
Token iniziali che ricevono molta attenzione anche se poco informativi, usati come ancora.

2611.29859.abs: Highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) has re-emerged as a One Health concern since 2024, and the public is increasingly consulting large-language-model (LLM) chatbots for health information during outbreaks. Before a chatbot's accuracy can be meaningfully assessed, its consistency must first be understood, so that any single response can be trusted as a fair representative of the model's behavior. We characterized the semantic repeatability and reproducibility of GPT-5 (OpenAI) and Gemini 3 Flash (Google) on 15 H5N1 One Health questions sourced from social media discourse by adopting and extending a centroid-based evaluation framework. Each question was submitted 30 times and reformulated using five Chain-of-Thought (CoT) variants with 30 runs each, yielding 5,400 responses. Pairwise cosine similarity was computed on MPNet embeddings, with sensitivity analyses across three additional transformers. Statistical inference combined standard nonparametric tests (paired Wilcoxon and Friedman with Holm--Bonferroni correction) with inter-embedding agreement statistics (ICC(2,k) and Cronbach's $α$) introduced here as a methodological addition. Both models produced high mean consistency (0.93--0.97, rescaled to {[}0, 1{]}). GPT-5 showed reproducibility significantly higher than repeatability (W = 3.0, p = 0.0003), whereas for Gemini 3 Flash the two metrics were statistically indistinguishable (W = 42.0, p = 0.33). Differential Diagnosis ranked among the top two CoT framings for consistency in both models. The tested chatbots behave as semantically stable sources on H5N1 One…

2611.30557.abs: Recent vision-language models (VLMs) can process hour-long videos, but the large number of input frames incurs substantial inference overhead. Existing approaches to efficient long-video understanding largely overlook video decoding, which can take longer than LLM prefill. We propose RAPID (Reference- and Access-Point-Informed Decoding), a codec-aware framework that exploits information embedded in compressed bitstreams to reduce both frame decoding and selection costs. RAPID consists of two components. RAPID-Dec exploits reference-frame information and random access points to skip unnecessary frames and decode the retained frames in parallel while preserving exact reconstruction of the target frames. It achieves up to a 3.7x decoding speedup over the fastest baseline on H.264/AVC videos. RAPID-Sel uses keyframes as coarse representatives of video segments, avoiding the dense candidate decoding and scoring required by existing frame selection methods. It achieves comparable accuracy with up to a 3.0x preprocessing speedup. Together, RAPID achieves a 4.9x time to first token (TTFT) speedup on hour-long videos over a state-of-the-art frame selection method using the fastest baseline decoder.

2611.31052.abs: Recommender systems exhibit popularity bias, often under-serving long-tail and cold-start items with sparse interaction data. We propose a group-specific data augmentation approach that leverages LLMs to generate synthetic interactions, formulated as a constrained optimization problem, maximizing group-specific NDCG@20 and coverage while bounding overall NDCG@20 degradation within an acceptable threshold. Items are partitioned by interaction frequency to find the optimal augmentation strategy for each group. We further study combining the augmentation across groups simultaneously and find that while individual optimal strategies navigate the multi-group augmentation design, they are not simply additive. We further ablate on the LLM-based augmentation itself, comparing LLM scales, augmentation configuration under token constraints, finding that augmentation quality scales with contextual richness, albeit at a proportionally higher cost. Experiments with SASRec demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, achieving over 100% and 60% improvement in group-specific NDCG@20 for extreme and regular long-tail items, respectively, on our industrial dataset, and 40%, 25% for MovieLens-32M, while increasing their coverage without significant overall degradation.

2611.30559.abs: Persistent tutoring agents do more than answer questions: they manage course files, practice records, and learner profiles that govern future lessons. In such stateful settings, knowing what to teach does not guarantee knowing what to change. We identify a pervasive failure mode, content-state decoupling, where agents deliver pedagogically sound responses while silently corrupting workspace state through unwarranted updates, missed prerequisites, or unintended side effects. Text-level judges overlook these state errors, whereas isolated tool-call checks break down because whether a write action is valid depends jointly on the learner request, prior state, and execution order. We propose State-Verified Reinforcement Learning, which supervises online policy optimization directly through verifiable workspace transitions. Within isolated sandboxes that snapshot state around every tool call, a deterministic verifier audits tool effects, workflow ordering, and native auto-sync side effects, pairing graded partial credit with a hard gate that zeroes episode reward upon any critical violation. Whenever no critical violation occurs, an evidence-grounded judge scores actual saved artifacts rather than agent claims. We pair 1,000 verifiable training instances with an independently authored, human-reviewed evaluation benchmark of 60 tasks spanning 11 educational categories and 16 native tools. After online GRPO training, Qwen3.8-27B raises category-weighted strict success on our benchmark from 51.47% to 80.74% (+29.27 points), cutting content-pass-only execution failures from 45.6% to…

2611.30605.abs: Diffusion-based graph generation models progressively transform Gaussian noise into structured graphs through stochastic dynamics. We observe that the effectiveness of this transformation is fundamentally determined by the evolution of the diffusion trajectory. Existing graph diffusion models often suffer from excessive uncertainty during diffusion and delayed growth of the signal-to-noise ratio, causing useful structural information to emerge only in the later stages of generation. To address this issue, we propose the Vasicek Graph Diffusion (VGD), a graph diffusion process derived from the Vasicek dynamics. The key insight of VGD is data-anchored mean dynamics with a closed-form solution, which analytically establishes a continuous transition from Gaussian noise to the target graph distribution. Unlike conventional graph diffusion processes that rely predominantly on stochastic evolution, VGD introduces a data-anchored drift that continuously steers the latent state toward the target distribution throughout diffusion. As a consequence, VGD maintains a smoothly evolving uncertainty while rapidly increasing the signal-to-noise ratio throughout diffusion, allowing informative graph structures to emerge much earlier during generation. Extensive experiments on multiple graph generation benchmarks demonstrate that VGD outperforms existing diffusion-based graph generative models in terms of generation quality and structural fidelity.

2611.30178.abs: Deploying large vision-language-action (VLA) models on resource-constrained robots demands extreme compression, yet existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods frequently collapse at ultra-low bit-widths ($\le$ 2 bits). We trace this failure to two mismatches in standard pipelines. First, calibrating on static offline demonstrations induces distribution shift: minor quantization perturbations drive the policy into unseen states where uncalibrated errors compound. Second, minimizing the layer-wise weight reconstruction error is a flawed proxy, as action generation depends only on the representations consumed by the action head. We present LoopQ, an on-policy ultra-low-bit quantization framework. LoopQ closes the loop by calibrating on states from the quantized policy's own rollouts. It then adds readout-aligned fine-tuning, which freezes the trellis codes and optimizes only lightweight lookup tables and scaling factors to align the backbone readout with the full-precision teacher. With all linear layers at 2 bits, LoopQ achieves a 60.4% success rate on LIBERO-Plus with GR00T N1.7, close to the 61.8% of full precision. Even at 1 bit per weight, $π_{0.5}$ still completes 80.0% of LIBERO tasks. With 8-bit activations, the 2-bit $π_{0.5}$ runs on integer kernels on an embedded NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor, with 4.1$\times$ smaller weights and 44% less memory. On a real AgileX Piper arm, it stays within one success of full precision on each of three tasks. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/LoopQ

ov.problema: Distribuire grandi modelli visione-linguaggio-azione (VLA: modelli che vedono, capiscono e producono azioni per robot) su robot con poche risorse richiede compressione estrema, ma la quantizzazione post-addestramento (PTQ) collassa a bit-width molto bassi (≤2 bit).
ov.idea: Gli autori individuano due cause: calibrare su dimostrazioni offline statiche crea distribution shift (le perturbazioni portano la policy in stati non visti), e minimizzare l'errore di ricostruzione dei pesi è un proxy sbagliato perché conta solo ciò che arriva alla testa d'azione. LoopQ calibra sulle rollout della policy quantizzata stessa e aggiunge un fine-tuning allineato alla readout, congelando i codici e ottimizzando solo lookup table e fattori di scala.
ov.risultati: Con tutti i layer lineari a 2 bit, LoopQ raggiunge il 60,4% di successo su LIBERO-Plus con GR00T N1.7, vicino al 61,8% della precisione piena. A 1 bit per peso, π0.5 completa ancora l'80,0% dei task LIBERO. Con attivazioni a 8 bit, il π0.5 a 2 bit gira su kernel interi su NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor, con pesi 4,1x più piccoli e 44% di memoria in meno.
ov.limiti: I risultati sono su benchmark e un braccio reale AgileX Piper con tre task; il testo è troncato.

glossario.d: Vision-Language-Action: modello che da immagini e istruzioni produce azioni per un robot.
Post-Training Quantization: riduzione della precisione dei pesi dopo l'addestramento.
Divergenza tra i dati di calibrazione e gli stati in cui il modello si trova davvero.

2611.30140.abs: Changing a graph embedding parameter can change what the layout represents. In SG-t-SNE-$Π$, the rescaling parameter $λ$ changes the probability assigned to each neighbor before optimization begins. We introduce LambdaLens to trace that change from individual edges to the resulting layout. For nodes with at least two neighbors, we derive a normalized power path. When the original weights are unequal, the number of neighbors determines where the weights become uniform and where their ordering reverses. Near $λ=1$, the rate of change in each edge probability depends on its surprisal relative to the neighborhood entropy. To measure the geometric effect, we vary $λ$ while holding the input graph, initialization, random seed, and optimizer settings fixed. Across six graphs, some layouts continue to move as $λ$ increases, others stabilize early, and others barely move. PubMed has the widest relative spread in node degree, yet its layout changes little. On four datasets with class labels, four probes recover 98.48-100% of the best label-fidelity score on a 16-value grid, using 75% fewer evaluations. In a six-dataset comparison, SG-t-SNE-$Π$ attains the highest observed primary score on four datasets and ranks among the top three on all six. On Citeseer, four probes come close to the dense-grid optimum, yet PHATE better preserves class structure, making a change of embedding pipeline worth considering on that graph. ```

2611.29613.abs: Web-scale recommender models evolve primarily through retraining or fine-tuning. We propose \emph{weight coding}, a methodology for model evolution through direct, executable weight edits. A large language model (LLM) agent inspects model structure and parameters, formulates hypotheses, and implements edits using evaluation feedback. The loop progresses from localized changes to targeted searches and composition, allowing edited components to adapt to one another. A cached engine enables rapid forward evaluation without backpropagation. On Pinterest's 147M-parameter Image Search two-tower retriever, weight coding improves held-out recall@10 of production model by up to 15.0 percentage points (+24\% relative) with few edits in about 1/4 GPU hours of a full post-training finetune, while a common launch only improves around 1\%. After reinitializing the entire 13.6M-parameter interaction module randomly while retaining the surrounding trained model, searching 2,448 mixing and normalization parameters yields 9.8 points above production. Offline gains span the full funnel including dense retrieval, generative retrieval and ranking, with up to 1.37B learnable parameters and different edits for each architecture. Steering edits provide explicit control of model performance over segments like freshness and product. Weight coding requires no serving change and online A/B tests increase saves per user from the edited retrieval source by 8.4\% to 10.7\%, aligned with the target business objectives. Our results establish weight coding as a practical and useful tool for model…

ov.problema: I modelli recommender su scala web evolvono principalmente tramite retraining o fine-tuning, processi costosi e lenti; serve un modo più diretto ed efficiente per migliorare le prestazioni.
ov.idea: Weight coding è una metodologia di evoluzione del modello tramite modifiche dirette ed eseguibili dei pesi. Un agente LLM ispeziona struttura e parametri, formula ipotesi e implementa modifiche usando feedback di valutazione; il ciclo va da cambiamenti localizzati a ricerche mirate e composizione, con un motore cached per valutazione forward rapida senza backpropagation.
ov.risultati: Sul retriever two-tower di Image Search di Pinterest (147M parametri), weight coding migliora il recall@10 held-out del modello di produzione fino a 15,0 punti percentuali (+24% relativo) con poche modifiche in circa 1/4 delle GPU-ore di un fine-tuning completo, mentre un lancio comune migliora circa l'1%. Dopo aver reinizializzato casualmente l'intero modulo di interazione (13,6M parametri) mantenendo il resto, cercare 2.448 parametri di mixing e normalizzazione dà 9,8 punti sopra produzione. I test A/B online aumentano i salvataggi per utente dalla fonte di retrieval editata dall'8,4% al…
ov.limiti: I guadagni offline coprono l'intera funnel con fino a 1,37B parametri apprendibili e modifiche diverse per architettura, ma non è chiaro quanto generalizzino oltre Pinterest o senza agente LLM.

glossario.d: Modello di retrieval con due torri separate per query e item.
Frazione di item rilevanti trovati tra i primi 10 risultati.
Evoluzione del modello tramite modifiche dirette dei pesi guidate da un agente LLM.

2611.30389.abs: Driving models need to choose which capabilities to use and when to reconsider their decisions. We introduce AgentMoT, a Mixture-of-Transformers with built-in agent reasoning and system scheduling. Combinations of agent, world, and action experts form three jointly trained pathways for direct-action, vision-language-action, and world-action computation. The Router selects a native pathway, while the agent expert supplies reasoning and selects skills. Execution feedback raises wake-up requests, and the agent self-scheduler learns whether to reconsider the task decision or keep it. Mandatory requests invoke the agent directly. The relative-capability principle guides these choices by relating the benefit of additional computation or intervention to its cost. After open-loop initialization, dual-loop evolution trains the Router, agent, and self-scheduler from closed-loop experience while failure-driven updates refine skills and execution feedback. AgentMoT achieves state-of-the-art results on Bench2Drive v0.0.3 and v0.0.4, with 94.48/92.33 driving score and 85.45/82.73% success rate, respectively. With skills disabled, learned routing improves over the strongest fixed pathway by 1.79 driving-score points and 4.09 percentage points of success rate on v0.0.3. Ablation studies further show gains from closed-loop agent learning, two-view queries, and event-triggered wake-up.

2611.28665.abs: Asking a vision-language model (VLM) to think step by step often makes it worse at spatial questions, even though the image stays in context. We show that short chain-of-thought (CoT) turns a perception problem into a transcription problem. Once a VLM writes a spatial relation, its answer follows that sentence instead of the image, so whether CoT helps or hurts depends largely on whether the written relation is more accurate than answering directly. Studying 15 open VLMs (2B-38B) and six frontier closed models, we rule out token count, turn format, and visual forgetting in open models and trace the failure through three stages. First, writing re-weights visual cues, weakening a "lower is closer" shortcut in all 13 open models tested but also discarding valid cues, which produces false relations. Second, the written text takes over. With the model's own conclusion-removed rationale held fixed, swapping in an opposite-depth image moves the answer by 2-9 points on rendered twins (vs. up to 77 for direct answers) and by 3.0-3.4 points on average on natural photographs (vs. 20.5-69.6). Third, the concluding sentence can invert even a true relation, mainly on converse questions. Together, false relations and conclusion mis-mapping account for four in five CoT losses. Scale does not remove this bottleneck: Qwen3-VL-32B shows the same pattern. Frontier closed models are not hurt: they write relations as accurately as they answer, and three of six re-check the image after writing. The three queried with reasoning off lock in like open models, so re-grounding co-occurs with…

ov.problema: Chiedere a un modello visione-linguaggio (VLM) di pensare passo per passo peggiora spesso le risposte a domande spaziali, anche se l'immagine resta nel contesto.
ov.idea: Gli autori mostrano che una breve catena di pensiero (CoT) trasforma un problema di percezione in un problema di trascrizione: una volta che il VLM scrive una relazione spaziale, la risposta segue quella frase invece dell'immagine. Il fallimento avviene in tre fasi: la scrittura ri-pesa gli indizi visivi, il testo scritto prende il sopravvento, e la frase conclusiva può invertire anche una relazione vera.
ov.risultati: Su 15 VLM aperti (2B-38B) e sei modelli frontier chiusi, scambiando l'immagine con una a profondità opposta si sposta la risposta di 2-9 punti su gemelli renderizzati (contro fino a 77 per risposte dirette) e di 3.0-3.4 punti in media su fotografie naturali (contro 20.5-69.6). Relazioni false e mappatura errata della conclusione spiegano quattro perdite CoT su cinque.
ov.limiti: I modelli frontier chiusi non sono danneggiati: scrivono relazioni accurate quanto le risposte e tre su sei ricontrollano l'immagine dopo aver scritto.

glossario.d: Modello che comprende sia immagini che testo
Far scrivere al modello i passaggi intermedi prima della risposta
Coppie di immagini sintetiche identiche tranne che per la profondità

2611.29813.abs: Real-time onboard robot control calls for a lightweight vision-language-action (VLA) model, yet shrinking the backbone leaves less capacity for deliberation at inference time. Chain-of-thought decoding, dual-system architectures, and larger backbones can restore deliberation but reintroduce the latency and memory costs that motivated going small. Recurrent action heads offer a lighter alternative by iterating in latent space before committing to an action, but existing designs refine a single undifferentiated state that must simultaneously encode slowly evolving task context and rapidly changing motor commands. We propose the Hierarchical Reasoning Action Head (HR-AH), which maintains two latent states updated at different frequencies: a low-level state that updates fast, grounded in action tokens and proprioception, and a high-level state that updates slowly, grounded in visual understanding and the instruction-informed low-level state. The two states exchange information through nested reasoning cycles. Because all iteration occurs in the compact head after a single backbone pass, HR-AH adds hierarchical reasoning without increasing the backbone size. With a 22.5M-parameter head, 3-4.3x smaller than those of RD-VLA and VLA-Adapter on the same backbone, HR-AH reaches 97.0% success rate on LIBERO and a 4.40 average chain length on CALVIN ABC->D, at the lowest latency among compared methods. We show that this hierarchy improves performance over a parameter-matched single-state head, and that routing distinct modalities to each level yields further gains in both accuracy and…

2611.30550.abs: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can execute individual skills but fail to complete tasks that require combining several of them. In our audit of Xiaomi-Robotics-1, an estimated 43\% of failures involve choosing the wrong target or losing track of task progress. Wrapping a frozen VLA in a vision-language model (VLM) harness is a natural remedy. Existing harnesses can gain substantially from task- and policy-specific preparation, raising the question of how much of that gain transfers to a new task or policy. An ideal harness should (i) need minimal preparation for a new task, (ii) need no redesign for a new policy, and (iii) preserve standalone capabilities the policy already has. To the best of our knowledge, our \ours{} is the first harness built this way. Its premise is that choosing targets and tracking progress are easy for a VLM such as GPT-6 without task preparation, while the frozen VLA already handles continuous, contact-rich motion. The frozen VLA therefore executes continuous control while the VLM plans zero-shot and monitors execution; when progress stalls or targets drift, the VLM first rephrases the instruction and, only as a fallback, executes short generated code over generic motion primitives before returning fine control to the VLA. The supervision rules stay fixed across policies, requiring only a thin interface adapter and an automatically profiled skill configuration per policy. On 200 RoboCasa365 scenes, \ours{} with GPT-6 Astra raises the success rate of frozen Xiaomi-Robotics-1 from \textbf{\color{blue}57.5\%} to \textbf{\color{blue}70.5\%} and…

2611.31027.abs: AI agents are given GPUs to do AI research on their own. Do they use those GPUs well? A busy GPU does not tell us, because it can be busy with work the answer did not need. This matters, because the tokens the agent spends cost almost nothing next to the GPUs its experiments run on, so using those GPUs better has a huge impact. So we built ComputeWise, an open benchmark of research tasks on which this waste can be measured and reduced. For it we developed our own simulated GPU, which replays recorded runs to the agent's code. With no real GPU needed, we ran hundreds of experiments, far more than would be reasonable on real GPUs. With no help, the agents put only 52% of their GPU time into work the answer needed. Another 22% went to work it did not need, and 26% sat idle. Asking the agent to finish the work faster, telling it to keep every GPU busy, or giving it a job scheduler does not fix this. So we built an open-source harness, part prompting and part deterministic code. Across five models, it removed over 80% of the extra time to the answer.

ov.problema: Gli agenti AI a cui vengono assegnate GPU per fare ricerca le usano in modo inefficiente: una GPU occupata non significa che stia svolgendo lavoro utile. Questo spreco è importante perché i token spesi dall'agente costano poco rispetto alle GPU, quindi usarle meglio ha un grande impatto.
ov.idea: ComputeWise è un benchmark aperto di compiti di ricerca per misurare e ridurre lo spreco. Include un simulatore di GPU che riproduce esecuzioni registrate, permettendo centinaia di esperimenti senza GPU reali. Hanno anche sviluppato un harness open-source (parte prompting, parte codice deterministico) che riduce il tempo extra per la risposta.
ov.risultati: Senza aiuto, gli agenti dedicano solo il 52% del tempo GPU a lavoro necessario, il 22% a lavoro non necessario e il 26% a inattività. L'harness rimuove oltre l'80% del tempo extra per la risposta su cinque modelli.
ov.limiti: Il simulatore potrebbe non catturare tutte le complessità delle GPU reali.

glossario.d: Strumento che combina prompting e codice per guidare l'agente.
GPU simulata che riproduce esecuzioni registrate senza hardware reale.

2611.30517.abs: Coding agents can now turn a well-specified ticket into a patch that passes its tests. Experienced engineers also notice risks the request never mentioned, question flawed premises, reuse what already exists and say plainly what they did and did not check. We present sudo L7, a benchmark of 60 software-engineering tasks written by staff-level engineers, mostly in private production codebases and each built around a place where a frontier model failed. A task pairs a realistic, underspecified request with a hidden, expert-authored rubric of atomic criteria (1,287 in all), tagged with eight behavioral dimensions from functional correctness to truthful reporting. An agentic grader reads the agent's transcript, inspects and runs its code, and treats test output as evidence. An attempt passes only if it meets every criterion of the two highest severities, and more than half of these gating criteria test something other than functional correctness. On the public leaderboard as of November 2026 (19 models, each in its developer's harness or in OpenCode, three attempts per task), Claude Fable 5.2 passes 52.2% of attempts, Claude Sonnet 5.5 50.6% and Claude Opus 5.5 46.1%. GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra pass 31-34%, and the other 13 models at most 18.9%. In a human-label study, three candidate model graders each agreed with a software engineer on 85-86% of criterion verdicts, about as often as two engineers agreed with each other. Cases from the benchmark show how one unsupported claim can fail an otherwise strong attempt and illustrate two sides of engineering…

ov.problema: Gli agenti di coding sanno trasformare un ticket ben specificato in una patch che passa i test, ma non si comportano come ingegneri esperti: non notano rischi non menzionati, non mettono in dubbio premesse sbagliate, non riusano ciò che esiste e non dichiarano cosa hanno controllato.
ov.idea: sudo L7 è un benchmark di 60 task di ingegneria del software scritti da ingegneri di livello staff, per lo più in codebase private di produzione, ognuno costruito attorno a un punto in cui un modello frontier ha fallito. Ogni task ha una richiesta realistica e sottospecificata e una rubrica nascosta di criteri atomici (1.287 in totale) su otto dimensioni comportamentali; un grader agentico legge il transcript, ispeziona ed esegue il codice e usa l'output dei test come evidenza.
